extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners to determine patent-eligible subject matter under the 2019 Patent Eligibility Guidance (2019 PEG), including how to identify whether a claim recites a judicial exception (Step 2A Prong One), how to evaluate integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two), groupings of abstract ideas, and related procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'recites' a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: In Step 2A Prong One, a claim 'recites' a judicial exception when the judicial exception is 'set forth' or 'described' in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two ways an exception can be recited: 'set forth' (explicitly stated, e.g., a mathematical equation) or 'described' (claimed concept expresses the exception without explicit terminology, e.g., 'intermediated settlement'). Examiner should evaluate whether the claim 'sets forth or describes' an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon per MPEP guidance and PEG examples (Examples 37-46, pre-PEG examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate recitation of a law of nature / natural phenomenon / product of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim sets forth or describes a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow MPEP 2106.04(b) and (c), including the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis. Use cited examples (Examples 43-45 and pre-PEG examples) to identify these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can recite more than one judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exceptions are distinct in different limitations, follow MPEP 2106.05(II). Do not 'parse' claims into separate abstract ideas when multiple abstract ideas are present; identify the claim as reciting each relevant exception for Step 2A Prong One, but, if possible, consider the limitations together as a single abstract idea for Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B (see Examples 45 and 46).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use enumerated groupings of abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify abstract ideas using the groupings enumerated in Section I of the 2019 PEG: mathematical concepts; certain methods of organizing human activity; and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groupings are grounded in case law and are not mutually exclusive; identify at least one grouping and preferably all that apply. If a limitation doesn't clearly fall within the enumerated groupings but case law indicates it is an abstract idea, bring the application to the TC Director per procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical concepts grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical concepts include mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining whether a claim recites a mathematical concept, consider whether the claim actually recites the concept rather than merely being based on or involving a mathematical concept. A mathematical relationship may be expressed in words or symbols (e.g., Arrhenius equation); numerical formulas or textual equivalents (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B') fall here; mathematical calculations encompass operations like multiplication or resampling statistics. See Examples 41, 43, 45 and MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships (subcategory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include relationships expressed by formulas (Arrhenius equation), conversions between numeral systems, or relationships between physical quantities. Recognize such relationships even if written descriptively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations (subcategory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical formulas or equations, including textual replacements of equations, are mathematical concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating force by multiplying mass by acceleration' are textual equivalents of equations and should be treated as formulas. See Parker v. Flook, Diamond v. Diehr examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations (subcategory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical calculations are mathematical operations or acts of calculating (e.g., multiplication, exponentiation, statistical analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim need not use the word 'calculating' to be a mathematical calculation; 'determining' or 'performing' may encompass calculations in the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim in light of the specification (see SAP Am., Inc. v. InvestPic, Inc. example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain methods of organizing human activity grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: This grouping covers enumerated sub-groupings: fundamental economic practices/principles; commercial or legal interactions; and managing personal behavior, relationships or interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all organizing methods are abstract ideas (e.g., specific drug formulation steps are not). This grouping is limited to the enumerated sub-groupings and should not be expanded except in rare cases (see Section III(C) of the PEG). The number of people involved is not dispositive; determine by whether the activity falls within a sub-grouping (see MPEP references and case examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles (subcategory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes subject matter relating to economy and commerce such as hedging, insurance, and mitigating risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Fundamental' does not mean 'old' necessarily, though age may be an indicator. Examples: hedging, offer-based price optimization, local processing of payments, certain clearinghouse/credit processing arrangements. See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(I) and cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions (subcategory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers agreements (contracts), legal obligations, advertising/marketing/sales behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transaction performance guaranty, processing insurance claims under a policy, tax-free real estate exchanges, arbitration, marketing techniques like offer-based price optimization, structuring sales forces. See cited cases and MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships (subcategory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes social activities, teaching, following rules or instructions, and interactions between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include voting/verification processes, sets of rules for games, assigning hair designs, instructions for hedging risk. See MPEP 2106.04(a)(2)(II)(C) and case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind (e.g., observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claim limitations can practically be performed in the human mind; if so, they fall within the mental processes grouping. Considerations: (i) if the limitation cannot practically be performed mentally (e.g., complex GPS pseudorange calculations, manipulation of network packets, specific data encryption, image halftoning), it is not a mental process; (ii) requiring a generic computer does not necessarily prevent classification as a mental process—an examiner should use the broadest reasonable interpretation in view of the specification; (iii) a claim encompassing human performance with pen and paper can recite a mental process. Use cited examples (Electric Power Group, University of Utah, CyberSource, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims requiring a computer may still recite mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that requires a generic computer can nonetheless recite a mental process if, in broad interpretation, the underlying concept is performable by the human mind and the computer is merely generic or a tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the specification to determine whether the invention is described as a concept performed in the mind and merely claimed as performed on a generic computer, in a computer environment, or using a computer as a tool. If so, treat as mental process (see Voter Verified and Mortgage Grader examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pen-and-paper aid does not negate mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim encompasses a human performing steps mentally with the aid of a pen and paper, it recites a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The use of a physical aid to assist memory does not change the mental nature of the limitation; however, if the limitation could not practically be performed in the human mind even with pen and paper, it is not a mental process (see CyberSource example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract idea procedure and TC Director review
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for handling claims that appear to recite an abstract idea not previously enumerated: TC Director approval is required for subject matter eligibility rejection based on a tentative abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office action will identify such claims via form paragraph 7.05.017 and include the TC Director’s signature; Patents Management is informed and public notification (e.g., USPTO.GOV/PatentEligibility) follows. Examiner retains authority to withdraw or maintain a rejection after applicant reply; an interview with the TC Director is not required to withdraw the rejection; interviews with the examiner may be conducted to advance prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two: 'integration into a practical application'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether the claim as a whole 'integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application' so that the claim imposes a meaningful limit on the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere recitation of an exception (Prong One) does not mean the claim is 'directed to' that exception. Use the considerations identified by the Supreme Court and Federal Circuit (improving technology, effecting a particular treatment/prophylaxis, using a particular machine, particular transformation, etc.) as set out in MPEP 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). If the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit (e.g., show an improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology), the claim is eligible at Step 2A; otherwise proceed to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or another technology or technical field as part of Prong Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the specification to see if it discloses sufficient details that an improvement would be apparent to a person of ordinary skill; the claim must reflect the disclosed improvement (but need not recite the improvement in explicit terms). Under the 2019 PEG, this Step 2A improvement analysis does not reference whether the improvement is conventional—showing an improvement to technology can be sufficient even if not an improvement over well-understood, routine, conventional activity. See SRI v. Cisco and life-sciences examples (CellzDirect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: particular machine or particular transformation and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a particular machine or a particular transformation and the specificity of limitations are considerations for integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'specific way of achieving a result' is not a standalone consideration, but the specificity of claim limitations is relevant to evaluating use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception. Generic computer components (e.g., 'data processing system') are insufficient by themselves to show integration (see CLS Bank example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-as-a-whole analysis (do not evaluate additional limitations in a vacuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two requires evaluating the claim as a whole — the judicial exception and additional claim elements together — to determine integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assess additional limitations entirely separate from the recited exception; consider how limitations interact and whether together they impose meaningful limits (see Bascom filtering example). If additional limitations are only insignificant extra-solution activity, proceed to Step 2B for conventionality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim integrates judicial exception at Step 2A, no further analysis required
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Prong Two evaluation shows the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application (e.g., by improving technology), the claim is eligible at Step 2A and the analysis ends there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include claims improving computer network technology where use of network monitors and integration of reports was held to constitute an improvement; conversely, generic computer components or mere instructions to implement on a computer require proceeding to Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: If an examiner identifies an abstract idea not clearly within enumerated groupings, raise to TC Director
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation does not fall clearly within the PEG enumerated groupings but case law suggests it is an abstract idea, the examiner should bring the matter to the TC Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'tentative abstract idea' procedure: TC Director approval for rejection, form paragraph, and public notification steps apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat a claim as reciting a mathematical concept if math only appears in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim does not recite a mathematical concept merely because the specification describes a mathematical concept; the mathematical concept must be recited in the claim itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations 'based on' or 'involving' a mathematical concept described in the specification may not suffice to place the limitation in the mathematical concepts grouping unless the math itself is recited in the claim; see Examples 38-39 guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap between Step 2A considerations and Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: Many considerations evaluated in revised Step 2A overlap with Step 2B; explanations in Step 2B rejections may be shorter because of this overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the examiner concluded in Step 2A Prong Two that an additional element was insignificant extra-solution activity, the examiner should re-evaluate in Step 2B whether that element is unconventional (i.e., more than well-understood, routine, conventional activity). Follow Berkheimer/HPE guidance and applicable memoranda when relying on conventionality findings.
